```{r, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Does a longer T-unit reflect more words, fewer counted structures, or a parser
decision that needs review? This guide keeps the original text, constituency
trees, matched nodes and denominators beside three English syntactic measures:
**MLC = W/C**, **MLT = W/T**, and **DC/C**. It then connects these results to
writer, task and occasion without dropping failed or absent submissions.

The helpers in `examples/l2sca.R` are explicitly
sourced installed examples. The separate Python runner calls a locally installed,
version-pinned original [L2 Syntactic Complexity Analyzer (L2SCA)](https://sites.psu.edu/xxl13/l2sca/).
The original software and models are not bundled or downloaded by ldfreq.
The runnable example below uses authored trees and declared matches, so it
requires neither Java nor a model. It demonstrates tracing and arithmetic,
not accuracy on learner writing or validity as a proficiency measure.

## Inspect an example before running a parser

```{r syntax-demo}
library(ldfreq)

demo <- new.env(parent = globalenv())
sys.source(system.file("examples", "l2sca-demo.R",
  package = "ldfreq", mustWork = TRUE), demo)
helper <- demo$helper
analysis <- demo$analysis
print(analysis$components[c("document_id", "W", "S", "C", "T", "DC", "status")],
  row.names = FALSE)
```

The fixture explicitly labels its provenance `authored-fixture`. Its rows
include finite and nonfinite complements, coordination, relative clauses,
fragments, an empty submission and a simulated process failure. Source text,
Penn trees and node IDs are available in the installed `l2sca-fixture.R`.
These declared structures do not imply that an automatic parser will assign
the same tree to every sentence.

| Component | Counting condition |
| --- | --- |
| W | Parser leaves whose POS is capital ASCII letters with an optional final `$`, and whose terminal text contains no parentheses or hyphen; equivalent to the pinned original word pattern on these trees |
| S | Top-level `ROOT` matches, including punctuation-only trees |
| C | Original clause matches `c` plus fragment correction `fc` |
| T | Original T-unit matches `t` plus fragment correction `ft` |
| DC | Original dependent-clause matches `dc` |

These are the pinned implementation's conditions. Consult [Lu (2010)](https://doi.org/10.1075/ijcl.15.4.02lu)
for the linguistic definitions; subsequent software contains additional query
rules. The runner reads the six original query constants from the original
script without importing or executing that script. The complete patterns are
saved in each real trace's provenance. Do not replace these counts with VERB,
`ccomp`, `xcomp` or `conj` counts from a dependency parser: those labels describe
different structures. Likewise, keep W separate from word counts in a lexical
diversity or readability analysis with different tokenization.

## Follow a value back to the source

```{r syntax-ratios}
print(subset(analysis$results,
  document_id %in% c("manual_coord_clauses", "manual_finite_complement", "manual_fragment_NP"),
  select = c("document_id", "measure", "numerator", "denominator",
    "original_rule_value", "value", "status")), row.names = FALSE)
print(subset(analysis$matches,
  document_id == "manual_coord_clauses" & pattern == "t",
  select = c("tree_id", "node_id", "start", "end", "source_span")), row.names = FALSE)
```

In `Maya reads, and Leo writes.`, the two T matches overlap: the whole sentence
and `Leo writes`. They are **query-matched subtrees**, not a partition into
nonoverlapping linguistic T-unit boundaries. MLT is the document's W divided
by T, here 5/2 = 2.5; averaging the words within those subtrees would give a
different statistic. Node IDs restart at each tree; token indexes and source
offsets run across the whole document. Offsets are one-based, inclusive Unicode
code-point positions, not byte offsets.

The importer passes parser leaves through `lexdiv_import_annotations()` to
check complete original-source coverage. It first tries literal surfaces, then
only the six explicit Penn bracket escapes (`-LRB-`, `-RRB-`, `-LSB-`, `-RSB-`,
`-LCB-`, `-RCB-`). Original leaves, decoded surfaces, conversion rules, offsets,
trees and matches remain available under `analysis$checked` and `analysis$matches`.
Only whitespace gaps are permitted. Other transformations are not guessed;
an unmatched leaf, omitted source text, malformed tree or parser fallback `X`
leaves that document `unusable_parse` with a reason and unchanged raw output.

An aligned tree can still be linguistically wrong. For example, the pinned
parser can split a closing curly quotation mark into a separate `ROOT`, and
can analyze a fragment as `NP` rather than `FRAG`. Review quotations, ellipsis,
fragments, segmentation and unusually short texts before reporting. No minimum
length filter is silently applied. All imported results initially say
`review_status = "not_reviewed"`.

## Run the original model locally and keep its output

Obtain `L2SCA-2023-08-15.tgz` from the [author's distribution page](https://sites.psu.edu/xxl13/l2sca/)
and follow its licensing conditions. That page labels the release 4.2.2;
the bundled README labels it 4.2.1. The archive SHA-256 is
`1cf48c2963b31182a4450e6e3298fbd2720a9c1cd08886029b41fe457d65b4f1`.
Retain your archive. The runner verifies hashes of `analyzeText.py`, Tregex,
the Stanford parser and its model jar before execution, and rejects changed
files. It uses the bundled Stanford 4.2.0 `englishPCFG` model and default parse
settings with explicit UTF-8 input/output. It is not a generic reader for other
L2SCA versions, parser models or languages.

Install Python 3 and Java separately, and ensure the `java` command works.
The parser is given a 1,500 MB Java heap, with additional process memory needed.
Each document is parsed separately; files are not concatenated to alter their
sentence boundaries. Local integration has been checked with Python 3.14 and
Java 11 on macOS. The R import example runs without those tools; successful
R checks on other platforms do not establish Java/model compatibility there.

Start with a complete original document table. Include submitted empty text as
`""`; an absent submission belongs in the planned study table, not as a fake
empty document. IDs must be unique nonblank strings, and text must be nonmissing
UTF-8. Additional research metadata stays in your independently saved roster.

```{r prepare-external, eval=FALSE}
helper <- new.env(parent = globalenv())
sys.source(system.file("examples", "l2sca.R", package = "ldfreq", mustWork = TRUE), helper)
documents <- data.frame(document_id = c("d1", "d2"),
  text = c("Maya reads books.", "Maya knows that Leo writes."))
saveRDS(documents, "original-documents.rds")
helper$l2sca_write_inputs(documents, "syntax-inputs.json") # optional jsonlite required
system.file("examples", "l2sca-trace.py", package = "ldfreq", mustWork = TRUE)
```

In a terminal, replace the two paths below with the printed runner path and
your extracted original directory. Quoting paths preserves spaces. The runner
uses only Python's standard library; it does not run an external shell script.

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
python3 "/path/to/ldfreq/examples/l2sca-trace.py" \
  --inputs "syntax-inputs.json" \
  --l2sca-dir "/path/to/L2SCA-2023-08-15" \
  --output "syntax-trace.json"
```

Both input writer and runner refuse to replace an existing output. Save to a
new file for a new run. Use `--java "/path/to/java"` if Java is not on PATH.
The trace contains original texts and their hashes, Penn output, each query's
tree/node IDs, process statuses, stdout/stderr, query definitions, model/tool
hashes and runtime versions. Do not share it if your source texts are private.
Captured output uses LF newlines. Invalid UTF-8 process output is retained as
base64 and marked failed rather than silently decoded into usable text.

```{r import-external, eval=FALSE}
documents <- readRDS("original-documents.rds")
analysis <- helper$l2sca_import("syntax-trace.json", documents)
analysis$components
analysis$results
analysis$matches
saveRDS(analysis, "syntax-analysis.rds", version = 2)
```

The independent roster must match the trace's complete ordered IDs and text.
Missing records, changed source/output hashes, incomplete successful-query
records and incompatible software identities stop import. Structural or
source-alignment problems retain the affected document with no usable values.
The default `max_nodes = 1000000` bounds total node reconstruction (including
terminals); a document that exceeds the remaining allowance has no reported
score, and nothing is silently truncated. Raw JSON is read into memory first;
this bound is not a general memory limit for arbitrary files.

Hashes detect accidental changes relative to the saved record. They are not
proof of authorship, model accuracy, or completeness against a maliciously
rewritten trace. The importer does not rerun Tregex to independently verify
every claimed match. Retain the original trace and the separately saved roster.

## Separate failures, undefined ratios and valid zero

| Status | Research value | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `computed` | Numeric, including DC/C = 0 | Successful traced computation; still needs scientific review |
| `no_words` | `NA` | W = 0 under these parser/counting conditions, including punctuation-only input |
| `zero_denominator` | `NA` | Nonempty text, but C or T is zero for that measure |
| `parser_failed`, `query_failed` | `NA`, with unavailable counts | External process failed; inspect its saved logs |
| `unusable_parse` | `NA`, with unavailable counts | Preserved tree, matches or source could not be reconciled |
| `not_submitted` | `NA` in study table | No document was supplied for the planned observation |

`original_rule_value` recomputes the original numerator/denominator rule,
including zero for a zero denominator. It is **unrounded and not an imported
official CSV score**. Keep an official CSV separately if comparing against its
four-decimal display. Failed documents have `NA` even in this column. A positive
denominator and DC = 0 is a valid zero, not missingness.

The original script can produce an all-zero CSV with exit status zero when an
input file is missing. A CSV or successful exit code alone therefore cannot
establish that the requested text was analyzed. This workflow requires source
identity, complete coverage, raw tree/query outputs and their statuses together.

## Carry review decisions and missing observations into a study

```{r syntax-study}
print(demo$review[c("document_id", "decision", "reason")], row.names = FALSE)
print(subset(demo$study_long, measure == "MLT",
  select = c("observation_id", "writer_id", "task", "occasion", "value",
    "status", "review_status", "report_value")), row.names = FALSE)
```

The example keeps a separate decision table keyed by document and `analysis_id`,
with reviewer and reason. It withholds one otherwise computed fragment by an
explicit illustrative reporting protocol. The original result remains intact.
Only a computed value with an explicit `include` decision enters `report_value`.
This approval is a documented human choice, not an automatic accuracy verdict.
Adapt the decision table after inspecting your own parses; do not copy the
fixture's decisions to real data.

`study_long` retains all 12 planned observations × 3 measures, including the
unsubmitted observation. Before fitting a model, choose one measure and one
analysis condition; the three measures from a document are not independent
observations. `demo$model_data` is an ordinary data frame containing only the
selected reportable MLT rows and their writer/task/occasion variables. It can be
passed to an existing modeling package. The tiny authored example is not fitted
to make inferential claims; use the [repeated-observations guide](repeated-observations.html)
to design an analysis with appropriate replication and random effects.

## Save and replay the full record

For research, replace `saved` below with a lasting private path such as
`"syntax-record.rds"`. Relative paths start at `getwd()`; temporary files
can disappear when R closes.

```{r syntax-replay}
saved <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
saveRDS(demo$record, saved, version = 2)
restored <- readRDS(saved)
helper$l2sca_validate(restored$analysis)
replayed <- helper$l2sca_import(restored$analysis$trace, restored$analysis$documents,
  max_nodes = restored$analysis$settings$max_nodes)
stopifnot(identical(replayed, restored$analysis))
```

In a fresh R session, use the same package snapshot and your saved path.
Inspecting the saved trace does not require Java or a parser model:

```{r resume-syntax, eval=FALSE}
library(ldfreq)
helper <- new.env(parent = globalenv())
sys.source(system.file("examples", "l2sca.R", package = "ldfreq",
  mustWork = TRUE), helper)
restored <- readRDS("syntax-record.rds")
helper$l2sca_validate(restored$analysis)
restored$analysis$components
restored$analysis$documents
restored$study_long
```

Save the trace, original roster, separate review decisions, study mapping and
complete RDS together. Flat tables alone omit trees and settings.
`l2sca_validate()` checks the imported record's saved integrity hash, including
its source, matches and scores. It does not validate separate reviewer decisions
or certify the scientific interpretation. Replay above reconstructs the same
results from saved output without invoking Java. Keep the ldfreq version and
session information when replaying in another environment.

The checks supporting this example distinguish three things: hand-declared
structures test the importer and arithmetic; pinned external runs and original
CSV comparisons test implementation agreement; neither is an independent
accuracy evaluation on learner writing. Such accuracy, proficiency and text
quality claims require evidence appropriate to the intended population and use.
